summary: This work shows that quantum error correction (QEC) cycles can be repurposed to programmably synthesize target dissipative dynamics at the logical level by treating the syndrome-averaged channel as a CPTP map and randomizing recovery operations. The framework enables resource-efficient simulation of open quantum systems on fault-tolerant devices through convex mixtures of implementable logical channels, avoiding explicit bath registers needed by dilation-based approaches.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures suppress all noise, but simulating real open quantum systems requires controlled dissipation as part of the target physics. Standard approaches embed dissipative channels into unitary evolution via Stinespring dilations, consuming $O(n)$ additional logical qubits for bath degrees of freedom; partial QEC instead converts calibrated noise into a programmable resource.
method: One QEC round (syndrome extraction, decoding, conditional recovery with discarded classical records) generates a CPTP logical channel $\mathcal{B}_d = \mathcal{D}_d \circ \mathcal{Q}_d \circ \mathcal{C}_d$. Randomizing the recovery operation or decoder over a library $\{\mathcal{G}_k\}$ produces convex mixtures $\mathcal{G}_r = \sum_k r_k \mathcal{G}_k$ that span Kraus channels. Target dissipators are compiled by solving a convex optimization problem in logical Choi space using Frank-Wolfe, with complexity scaling as $\mathcal{O}(LM^2(d)/\eta)$ in library size $M(d)$ rather than physical Hilbert-space dimension.
result: For two-site exciton dynamics with dephasing and amplitude damping ($\gamma_j$, $\gamma_{12}$, $\kappa_j$ rates), Strategy A (model-aware, using calibrated physical noise) and Strategy B (post-correction programming) both achieve trace distance $\lesssim 1\%$ from exact Lindblad evolution. Strategy A reduces code distance by setting it to uncontrolled errors only (Eq. 20: $\epsilon_\mathrm{un}(d) + \epsilon_\mathrm{prog}^A + \nu_d \lesssim \zeta \Delta_\mathrm{tar}(\tau)$), yielding qubit overhead scaling as $[d(x_B)/d(x_A)]^2$ with target-aware threshold $x_A = \zeta \Delta_\mathrm{tar}(\tau) \gg \epsilon/m = x_B$; Strategy B avoids model-calibration sensitivity and eliminates bath ancillas.
